newsitem.title: FRANCE: France may bend advertising rules for World Cup.
newsitem.headline: France may bend advertising rules for World Cup.

text.p: France may bend its rules barring alcoholic drink ads from being shown on television during the World Cup soccer championship to accommodate sponsors such as U.S. brewer Anheuser-Busch, a government source said on Thursday.

"The solution envisaged by the ministries concerned would be an amendment to the audiovisual code of conduct to permit television channels to broadcast sports events even if the billboards shown breach the 1991 law," the source told Reuters.
The 1991 Evin law bans advertisements for alcoholic drinks from French television. Even billboards on stadium walls cannot appear.
Anheuser-Busch, which makes Budweiser beer, had asked the government to make an exception during the 1998 World Cup football tournament or interpret the rule less harshly.
Anheuser-Busch is a big sponsor and has signed a 100 million franc ($17.3 million) contract with the world football federation FIFA.
Officials at the ministries of youth and culture and sports declined comment.

But French drinks producers blasted the government for considering an exception for the World Cup when it has been indifferent to the French industry's troubles. The law makes it hard for French drinks companies to put up billboards during sports events abroad that are shown on French TV.
A group of French wine, beer and spirits producers said in a statement that the government's move "to make an exception so that a foreign brand can be shown on French screens" was absurd.
While there was no evidence that the Evin law contributed to reducing alcohol abuse, "the law exists and it is essential that it be at least fairly applied to all," it said.
